Hello all!

I am having some difficulties with importing Tasks from a .csv file.

I am trying to import two tasks, “Import Test Parent” and “Import Test Child”, such that “Import Test Child” has “Import Test Parent” as a dependent task.

I can do this with two separate imports:

"ID","Subject","Task (Dependent Tasks)"
"CUSTID-TASK-2025-00002","Import Test Parent",""

and

"ID","Subject","Task (Dependent Tasks)"
"CUSTID-TASK-2025-00003","Import Test Child","CUSTID-TASK-2025-00002"

but of course in practice, there may be much longer chains of tasks than this and having a separate import for every level of dependency would be annoyingly time-consuming.

I tried importing this .csv:

"ID","Subject","Task (Dependent Tasks)"
"CUSTID-TASK-2025-00002","Import Test Parent",""
"CUSTID-TASK-2025-00003","Import Test Child","CUSTID-TASK-2025-00002"

but because “CUSTID-TASK-2025-00002” did not exist in the database yet, the system simply refused to import at all - even though it WOULD appear if imported in order.

Am I doing something wrong here? Is there a way to import tasks with dependencies? Any help is appreciated!

posts.name: Sudhanshu Badole
posts.cooked:
@TSping1
When importing tasks with dependencies in Frappe, the Data Import Tool validates all linked fields before inserting any records. This means that if a parent task does not already exist in the database, the import will fail even if that parent is included earlier in the same CSV. The most reliable way to handle this is by using a two-pass import. In the first pass, you import all tasks with just their IDs and Subjects while leaving the dependency column blank so that every task is created in the system. In the second pass, you re-import the same tasks, this time filling in the dependency field. Since the parent tasks now exist, the validation will succeed and the dependencies will be linked correctly. This method is the best because it is simple, safe, and scalable, no matter how long the chain of tasks is, and it avoids the need for complex scripting or multiple imports for each level of dependency.

posts.name: Sudhanshu Badole
posts.cooked:
@Peer
Not really — Frappe doesn’t spell this out anywhere as an “official SOP.” The Data Import Tool was designed with a pretty strict validation-first model: every link must exist in the database before the importer lets the row in. That’s great for data integrity, but it means imports with self-referencing or chained dependencies (like tasks, BOMs, or hierarchical projects) don’t work in a single shot.

What I suggested — the two-pass approach — is more of a community-proven workaround than a published rule. People who’ve run into this issue (tasks, dependent items, parent–child structures) have figured out that splitting the import into “create everything first” and “link everything second” is the cleanest way to align with how the importer works internally.

So, no, it’s not in the manuals as an SOP, but yes, it’s the practical standard that experienced Frappe/ERPNext users follow when importing linked data. You’ll find the same advice floating around in forum threads and issue discussions.

It found myself inserting “sleep(X)” lines because some job was slow to add parents which were needed just some lines later but not yet present when arrived there. So slowing down “helped”, but unsatisfactorily.

Anyway, if it works, I don’t care that much if it’s “official”.

But it’s not that simple.
If the underlying framework changes, “official” might prove more stable over time, because it better fits to implied “contracts” of stability over time which the developing/maintaining/supporting devs know best, at least better than what a non-connected (more independent than the internal or gameplanned ones) dev can know due to the distance to the inner circle. (Which, of course, also is a relative statement, “breaking changes” also being an official reality.)

This probably always exists in any group, simply due to normal human communication reach limitations: very rare probably are those who can meaningfully, constantly and consistently over time communicate with the whole dev ecosystem, knowing everybody very well as well as their project’s states, plans and intentions over time, in order to implicate themselves/collaborate like a glove on a hand in all the projects. Expecting this seems like pure fantasy to me, so we must be quite self-sufficient, self-evolving, and make do with less than total communication and knowledge, and everyone must find their methods and ways to contact people meaningfully and usefully on a much humbler scale than “total”.
